title: People-Machinery Interaction
body: Most people-machinery incidents come from one failure: someone walks into a machine's working zone without the operator knowing. At ADW that cost us a supervisor in September, terminated after approaching a running 398 excavator without radio contact, and DT-128 showed what a fatigued operator does to a high wall.
keyPoints: Three universal rules: the operator must have seen you, you wait for the machine to park with GET on the ground and a signal to approach, and no vehicle parks behind operating equipment.
Approach a running excavator in three checkpoints: radio at 50 m, confirm bucket down at 30 m, confirm operator out of the cab at 10 m.
No radio contact means you stop and wait in your vehicle. Richard's own words after the 398 interview: "I should have stayed in my vehicle and waited."
A busy radio is not an excuse. Saud confirmed the channel was clear and Richard still didn't answer.
In the mining area, headlights and amber strobes stay on, and windows, mirrors and taillights stay clean. If any fail, park the machine and raise it.
Fatigue is part of this rule. DT-128 fell asleep loaded, and fatigue reporting is still not trusted on site.
apply: Watch light vehicles and supervisors approaching the loading faces and ROM pad during handover and after dark, and check whether they call by radio at 50 m before they close in.
